E2A:
So some very practical questions to ask when one is asking "Is this person good enough?" might be, "How much attention can this person bring to other people right now? How available is he or she to engage in self-examination? And how available are we to this person, without being taken over by him or her?"

Some people have engaged in long practices of contemplation or therapy, or have had very good luck in childhood; other people are just trying to survive some emergency in their life. Most of us are all of these at different times in our lives.

E3A:
In the model I’m imagining, some of the functions that are outsourced to therapists in modern society are distributed throughout the community. In other words, there’s a lot of peer counseling going on.

But it’s not infinite.

I’m going to use the phrase “free resource,” which comes from Re-evaluation Counseling, to refer to the capacity people have to help others, and “need” to refer to the amount of help people need at a given time.

Everyone has a certain amount of both, and the ratio varies.
E3B:

But there are limits to that distribution.

I'll use the Re-evaluation Counseling term of free resource to describe the ability to be there for others. Free resource is in a kind of see-saw relationship with need, the amount of help one needs at a given time.

All of use have both.

E5A:
The problem is that, in a group of eight people, if two are in a sustained crisis mode, the group ends up spending most of its resources to care for those in crisis. However, in a group of eighty people, the crisis can be distributed amongst the group.

The problem is one of resources -- how many people can a group take in without hurting the existing members or the people they are taking in?
E5B:
One of the reasons a large group is sometimes able to deal with crisis/need is, that the larger the group the better chance some of the members are not effected by the crisis. A group of 8, that has 2 people in a sustained crisis, will spend most of it's time supporting those two. The same group of 80, can spread the load out more easily.

Welcome is a question of resources. Welcoming someone without resources to offer, will likely cause damage to the people already present and possibly to the welcomed one.

E6B:
There is a difficult paradox to consider. The need for new members in a small community is greater, but the ability of that community to tolerate the disruption of new members is less. Whether there are eight people in the community or eight hundred, someone still has to grow the food, fix the cars, balance the books, watch the kids, and maintain the water system. The water well doesn’t care how beautiful someone’s heart is.

Early on, members need to have more resource than need, and some skill to contribute, but at least a willingness to learn is important.
E7A: I still have no good answer for how to wield this power in a way that does not simply become an excuse to exclude disabled people, or poor people, or people who can’t speak the language of therapy, or people who are just…well, simply for basically any group of people who are not convenient. And it can’t be solved by pretending that there is no limit to my capacity. It has to have concrete criteria, and review from outside, and ways to appeal the decision that someone is not worth my time right now. But it is dangerous.
E7B: How to use the framing of “I don’t have the capacity to…” in a way that does not exclude disabled people, poor people, people who don’t have the language of therapy at their fingertips, people who are simply not convenient for me – I don’t know. It’s not going to be solved by pretending it’s unlimited and can be used at any time; that’s going to require actually making concrete criteria, allowing for outside review of those criteria, allowing for re-visiting a “not now” decision, and all of that.
E8A:
You may not be a good fit for this community right now if:

You’re running for your life from something and need a place to land, get treatment, housing, legal aid, etc. (It’s good that some groups can provide this, but it’s not what the group that founded this site is trying to pretend to do.)

You want all of the benefits of village life but don’t want to take on governance, maintenance, conflict, care, etc.

You’re not willing to look at yourself when jealousy or conflict comes up.

You have a need that far outstrips your ability to bring in a resource for it right now. (This doesn’t mean you’re bad or doomed; it may mean you need to take a first step of finding support where you are so you can build up your resources a bit.)

(There are probably ways of not flat-out rejecting people who fall into these categories, which would be good to come up with.)
E8B:
You may not be ready for a community like this if:

You're running from a difficult situation in search of a safe place to get treatment, housing or legal support etc, this is not what a community in its founding stages is.

You want to live in a village where someone else is in charge.

You're not willing to self reflect in times of jealousy and conflict.

You have a huge need right now, but little resource to meet it, you're probably not worthless, but may need to take the first step where you are.

These can all be handled with good membership processes rather than simply saying no.
